set.detail: The Lombards had settled in Pannonia under Justinian as federates against the Gepids, and 5,500 of them fought for Narses at Taginae. In 567 their king Alboin, allied with the Avars of Bayan, destroyed the Gepid kingdom, killed the Gepid king Cunimund, made a drinking cup of his skull and married his daughter Rosamund. Facing the powerful Avars as neighbours, Alboin led his people into Italy, leaving Pannonia to the Avars by a treaty that Paul the Deacon says reserved the Lombards' right to return within 200 years. On Easter Monday, 2 April 568 (Paul's date, often corrected to 569 from Marius of Avenches), a mixed host of Lombards, Saxons (20,000 according to Paul), Gepids, Bulgars, Sarmatians, Pannonians, Suebi and Noricans crossed the Julian Alps into Friuli. Paul records the legend that Narses, dismissed by Justin II and insulted by Sophia, who sent him a spindle, had invited them. Italy, exhausted by the Gothic war and plague, offered little resistance: Forum Iulii (Cividale) became the first Lombard duchy under Alboin's nephew Gisulf, Milan fell in September 569, and Pavia after a three-year siege in 572. The Roman administration under the prefect Longinus held only fortified coastal cities, Ravenna, Rome and Naples. Alboin was murdered in 572 by Rosamund and her lover Helmichis, and after the brief reign of Cleph the Lombards were ruled by dukes for ten years. The invasion ended the political unity of Italy, which would not be restored until 1861, and created a lasting division between Lombard and Byzantine territories, including the exarchate of Ravenna, the duchy of Rome and the southern duchies, that shaped Italian history for centuries.
set.debate: Date (568 or 569) and the story of Narses's invitation are disputed.

scholarship: Christie, The Lombards (1995)
Pohl, 'The empire and the Lombards', in Pohl (ed.), Kingdoms of the Empire (1997)
Wickham, Early Medieval Italy (1981)

set.detail: The Fifty Years' Peace of 562 obliged Rome to pay Persia 30,000 solidi a year, with the first seven and then three years paid in advance. Justin II, who had refused the Avar subsidies on his accession, regarded these payments as humiliating tribute. Several developments made war attractive. The Western Turks, who had destroyed the Hephthalites with Persia and then quarrelled with Khosrow over the silk trade, sent an embassy under the Sogdian Maniakh to Constantinople in 568, and Justin sent Zemarchus in 569 to the court of Istämi, creating an alliance to encircle Persia. In Persarmenia, the Armenian prince Vardan Mamikonian led a revolt and killed the Persian governor Chihor-Vishnasp (Suren) at Dvin in February 572, appealing to Justin for help as a fellow Christian. Iberia was also restive. Justin refused to pay the annual sum due in 572 and declared his support for the Armenians, despite the treaty's prohibition on receiving subjects of the other. The Roman general Marcian, Justin's cousin, raided Arzanene in 572 and besieged Nisibis in 573, while the Persians under Khosrow I counter-attacked, taking Dara and raiding Syria under Adarmahan. The war of 572-591 thus began with an act of aggression by Justin, contrary to the advice of his ministers, and turned out disastrously: the Turkish alliance collapsed after Justin's ambassadors were humiliated in 576, the loss of Dara drove the emperor mad, and the war lasted almost twenty years, ending only when the Persian civil war gave Maurice the chance to restore Khosrow II in 591. Evagrius and John of Ephesus blame Justin's arrogance, while Theophylact presents the war as a Roman defence of Christian Armenians.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Turtledove, 'Justin II's observance of Justinian's Persian treaty', BZ 76 (1983)

set.detail: Dara, the fortress built by Anastasius in 505 at Anastasiopolis to face Nisibis, was the keystone of the Roman defence of Mesopotamia; its walls, cisterns and dams had been rebuilt by Justinian, and its existence had been a grievance of the Persians since its foundation. After the panic and collapse of the Roman siege of Nisibis in spring 573, Khosrow I, aged over seventy, led his army in person to Dara, while his general Adarmahan raided Syria. The siege lasted about six months. Khosrow diverted the river that supplied the city and built siege mounds; the defenders were hampered by the weakness of the imperial response, as Justin had recalled Marcian and no relief army came. The city fell in November 573, betrayed according to some sources, after the Persians took a section of the wall on the mound. The Persians massacred many of the inhabitants and deported the rest; John of Ephesus claims that among the deportees were girls whom Khosrow sent to the Turks, and who drowned themselves in a river rather than suffer. The loss of Dara was a catastrophe: it was the first major Roman city in Mesopotamia captured permanently since Amida in 503, and it opened Roman territory to further raids. When Justin II heard the news, Evagrius says, he went mad; his wife Sophia took power and bought a truce. The return of Dara became the key demand of Roman negotiators, and it was finally obtained only in 591 when Maurice restored Khosrow II, who ceded Dara and Martyropolis. Khosrow II took Dara again in 604.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Croke and Crow, 'Procopius and Dara', JRS 73 (1983)

set.detail: Slavs (Sclaveni and Antes) had raided south of the Danube since Justinian's early years, but in the 570s and 580s, while Roman armies were fighting the Persians, they began to settle permanently. John of Ephesus, writing around 584, says that in the third year of Tiberius (581) the 'accursed people of the Slavs' overran all Greece, Thessaly and Thrace, taking many cities and forts, devastating, burning and enslaving, and that they now lived in Roman territory without fear, as in their own land, had grown rich in gold and silver, horses and weapons, and had learned to fight better than the Romans. Evagrius records that the Avars, with Slavs, reached the Long Walls and took Singidunum, Anchialus and the whole of Greece. The Chronicle of Monemvasia, a later and controversial text, records that the Avars and Slavs conquered the Peloponnese in the sixth year of Maurice (587-588) and held it for 218 years, the inhabitants of Patras fleeing to Rhegium and those of Lacedaemon to Sicily or to Monemvasia, the 'single entrance' rock. Archaeology shows the abandonment of many settlements and the appearance of Slavic-style handmade pottery and cremation burials at Olympia and elsewhere, though the dating and interpretation are disputed. The Miracles of St Demetrius describe Slavic sieges of Thessalonica and settled Slavic tribes around the city. The scale of the settlement was debated in the nineteenth century by Fallmerayer, who claimed the Greeks had been replaced by Slavs. Modern scholarship accepts large-scale Slavic settlement in the Balkans and parts of Greece from the 580s, with Roman control limited to coastal cities until the Byzantine reconquest in the late eighth and ninth centuries.
set.debate: The Chronicle of Monemvasia's reliability and the date and scale of Slav settlement in the Peloponnese are disputed.

scholarship: Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Avramea, Le Péloponnèse du IVe au VIIIe siècle (1997)

set.detail: Sirmium, once one of the imperial capitals of the tetrarchy and the seat of the prefecture of Illyricum, had been held by the Gepids until 567, when, after their destruction by the Lombards and Avars, the Romans recovered it. Bayan, the Avar khagan, claimed it as part of the Gepid inheritance. In 579 the Avars, with the help of Roman craftsmen requisitioned on the pretext of building baths, built two bridges across the Sava, one above and one below the city, and blockaded it. Menander, the main source, describes the long negotiations: Tiberius II, whose armies were committed to the Persian war, sent envoys and offered subsidies; Bayan swore on a sword and on the Gospels that he did not intend to attack Roman territory. The garrison and people suffered from hunger. Tiberius tried to send troops under Theognis, but they were too few. In 582 Tiberius agreed to surrender the city; the inhabitants were allowed to leave with nothing but their clothes, and the Avars received the arrears of their annual subsidy of 80,000 solidi for three years. Sirmium was abandoned; excavations show a sharp break at the end of the sixth century. A brick from Sirmium bears a scratched inscription in Greek: 'Lord, help the city and stop the Avars, and protect Romania and the writer. Amen.' The fall of Sirmium gave the Avars a base on the Danube frontier and opened the way for their attacks on Singidunum, Viminacium and the Balkan interior in the following years, and is often seen as the beginning of the collapse of the Roman Danube frontier.
set.debate: The famous brick inscription's date and authenticity have been questioned but are generally accepted.

scholarship: Pohl, The Avars: A Steppe Empire in Central Europe 567-822 (2018)
Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)

set.detail: Gregory, born around 540 into a senatorial family of Rome that had produced Pope Felix III, was urban prefect around 573, then gave away his property, founded monasteries in Sicily and on his family estate on the Caelian hill (St Andrew's) and became a monk. Pope Pelagius II made him deacon and sent him to Constantinople as apocrisiarius (579-586), where he debated with the patriarch Eutychius and began his Moralia on Job. Elected pope after Pelagius died of plague in February 590, he hesitated, reportedly wrote to Maurice asking him to refuse confirmation, and was consecrated on 3 September 590. His fourteen-year pontificate shaped the medieval papacy. With Rome threatened by the Lombards and the exarch in Ravenna unable to defend it, Gregory organised the defence of the city, paid troops, negotiated with Agilulf in 593 and 598, and managed the vast estates of the Roman church in Sicily, southern Italy, Dalmatia, Gaul and Africa, the patrimony of St Peter, which supplied grain to Rome. His 850 surviving letters show him intervening in the affairs of churches from Spain to Constantinople, protesting against the patriarch John the Faster's title of ecumenical patriarch and calling himself servant of the servants of God. He sent Augustine and forty monks to convert the English in 596-597. He wrote the Pastoral Rule (591), a handbook for bishops, the Dialogues (593-594), homilies on the Gospels and Ezekiel, and was later credited with the reform of liturgical chant. He died on 12 March 604 and became one of the four Latin Doctors of the Church.

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

scholarship: Markus, Gregory the Great and His World (1997)
Richards, Consul of God (1980)
Straw, Gregory the Great: Perfection in Imperfection (1988)

set.detail: In 590 the Persian general Bahram Chobin, humiliated by Hormizd IV after a defeat by the Romans in the Caucasus, rebelled and marched on Ctesiphon. A palace coup overthrew Hormizd and placed his son Khosrow II on the throne, but Bahram defeated Khosrow on the Nahrawan canal and seized the throne himself as Bahram VI, the first non-Sasanian king. Khosrow fled with a few followers to Roman territory at Circesium and appealed to Maurice, offering Dara, Martyropolis and much of Armenia in return for help. Against the advice of his senators, who argued that letting the Persians fight each other was better, Maurice agreed, perhaps seeing the chance of peace on the eastern frontier after twenty years of war, and Khosrow was given an army. In 591 a Roman army under Narses, magister militum per Orientem, and the Armenian John Mystacon, with Armenian troops under Mushegh Mamikonian and Persian loyalists led by Khosrow's uncles Vistahm and Vinduyih, invaded Persia through Armenia and Atropatene. They met Bahram on the river Blarathon near Ganzak in Atropatene in late summer 591. Bahram's forces, including elephants, were defeated after a hard fight; Theophylact says the Romans captured his elephants and that Bahram fled to the Turks in Central Asia, where he was assassinated in 592 at Khosrow's instigation. Khosrow was restored to the throne and, in the peace of 591, ceded Dara, Martyropolis, much of Persarmenia including Dvin, and Iberia up to Tiflis to the Romans, without annual payments. It was the most favourable treaty Rome had ever made with Persia, but Khosrow II's debt to Maurice became the pretext for the devastating war of 603-628.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008)

set.detail: In 598 Maurice and the khagan Bayan concluded a peace that allowed the Romans to cross the Danube to fight the Slavs. In 599 Maurice broke it, perhaps after Bayan's demands, and ordered Priscus, magister militum per Thracias, to cross the Danube into Avar territory at Viminacium, while Comentiolus led a second army. Theophylact describes a campaign of several battles on the Pannonian plain north of the river. Priscus's army, transported across the Danube on boats, won a series of victories over the Avars near Viminacium; in the first, the khagan's four sons were killed, according to Theophylact, and the Avars lost 4,000 men. Priscus then won two further battles and pursued the khagan towards the Tisza, where in a fifth engagement 3,000 Avars, 8,000 Slavs and 6,200 other barbarians were captured and some 30,000 enemies killed. Gepid villages were destroyed. The prisoners were sent to Tomis, but Maurice ordered them returned to the khagan as part of a settlement, a decision that angered the army. Theophylact's figures are exaggerated, but the campaign showed that the Roman army under competent leadership could defeat the Avars in their own territory and was the high point of Maurice's Balkan war. In 600 Bayan's counter-offensive in Dalmatia and the plague in his army weakened the Avars further. However, the army's exhaustion and resentment at Maurice's economy measures, including orders to winter north of the Danube, led to the mutiny of 602, the overthrow of Maurice and the end of the Roman offensive. Within two decades the Avars were besieging Constantinople.
set.debate: Theophylact's casualty figures are untrustworthy; Whitby dates the campaign to 599.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Pohl, The Avars (2018)
Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)

set.detail: The Strategikon is a military manual in twelve books written in Greek around 592-610, traditionally attributed to Maurice, who may have commissioned or contributed to it, although some manuscripts name an Urbicius and others attribute it to Maurice's brother-in-law Philippicus. It is the most important source on the late Roman army. Books 1-3 deal with the organisation and training of the cavalry, by then the main striking force: the army is divided into moirai and banda of 200-400 men, armed with bow and lance, wearing mail and helmets, using stirrups (first mentioned in Byzantine sources), and drilling with Latin commands such as 'cede', 'iunge', 'deus adiuta'. Books 4-10 cover ambushes, baggage, marches, camps, sieges and the general's conduct, with maxims. Book 11 describes the characteristics and tactics of the enemies of the Romans: Persians, 'Scythians' (Avars and Turks), 'light-haired peoples' (Franks and Lombards), and Slavs and Antes, who live in forests and marshes, are disorderly, hospitable to strangers, and should be attacked in winter when the trees are bare and the rivers frozen. Book 12 covers infantry formations, drill and camps, including a Latin and Greek vocabulary of commands. The Strategikon shows a professional army adapted to fight steppe nomads by adopting their methods, with emphasis on careful planning, intelligence, deception and avoidance of risky pitched battles. It was the basis of later Byzantine military manuals such as the Taktika of Leo VI. Its Latin commands show that Latin remained the language of the army a century after it had disappeared as the administrative language of the eastern empire.
set.debate: Authorship (Maurice, Philippicus or an anonymous officer) and the date (590s or early seventh century) are debated.

scholarship: Dennis, Maurice's Strategikon (1984)
Rance, 'Drungus, Droungos and Droungisti', GRBS 46 (2006)
Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World (1999)

set.detail: Maurice's Balkan campaigns had restored Roman control of the Danube by 600, but at great cost, and his attempts to reduce military expenditure had already caused a mutiny in the eastern army in 588 and unrest in the Balkans. In autumn 602 he ordered the army under his brother Peter to winter north of the Danube in Slav territory, to save money and to feed off the enemy's land. The soldiers, exhausted and fearing the cold, mutinied; they raised on a shield the centurion Phocas, a junior officer of Thracian origin who had previously been part of a delegation of soldiers to Maurice, when he was humiliated by the patrician Comentiolus. The army marched on Constantinople. Maurice tried to defend the city with the circus factions, but the Greens turned against him; on the night of 22 November he fled by boat with his family to Asia, sending his son Theodosius to Persia to seek help from Khosrow II. The army and the Greens first offered the throne to Germanus, Theodosius's father-in-law, who refused, and then Phocas, who was crowned in the church of St John the Baptist at the Hebdomon by the patriarch Cyriacus on 23 November and entered the capital the next day. Phocas ordered the execution of Maurice and his sons. His eight-year reign was remembered by later sources, partly written under Heraclius, as a tyranny of terror, executions and military disaster, as the Persians invaded the East and the Avars and Slavs overran the Balkans. Modern historians see the revolt of 602 as a turning point: the first violent overthrow of an emperor in Constantinople since its foundation, it opened a period of civil war and external invasion that nearly destroyed the empire.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)
Kaegi, Byzantine Military Unrest 471-843 (1981)

set.detail: After his flight across the Bosporus on 22 November 602, Maurice, suffering from gout, stopped at the church of St Autonomus near Praenetus (or at Chalcedon) with his wife Constantina and their children; his eldest son and co-emperor Theodosius had been sent towards Persia. Phocas, crowned on 23 November, sent the officer Lilius with soldiers to seize them. On 27 November 602, at the harbour of Eutropius at Chalcedon, they executed his five younger sons, Tiberius, Petrus, Paulus, Justinus and Justinianus, one after another before his eyes, and then Maurice himself. Theophylact records that Maurice repeated the verse of Psalm 119 'Righteous art thou, O Lord, and upright are thy judgements', and that when a nurse tried to substitute her own child for one of his sons, Maurice refused to allow it and handed over his own son. The heads were displayed on the Tribunal at the Hebdomon until they began to rot, and the bodies were thrown into the sea; Theodosius was captured and executed near Nicaea, as were Maurice's brother Peter and the general Comentiolus. Constantina and her daughters were confined in a monastery and executed some years later. The murder of a legitimate emperor and his family shocked contemporaries; Khosrow II, who owed his throne to Maurice, used it as the pretext for war and sponsored a pretender claiming to be Theodosius. Later Byzantine sources, written under Heraclius, portrayed Maurice as a pious martyr and Phocas as a monster, and Maurice was venerated as a saint in the Orthodox church. The details of the execution are in Theophylact and the Chronicon Paschale.

scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and His Historian (1988)
Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)

set.detail: Khosrow II, restored to power by Maurice in 591, had maintained peace for a decade, keeping good relations with the emperor, whom he called his father. When news of Maurice's execution arrived, Khosrow imprisoned Phocas's envoy Lilius and declared war in 603, presenting himself as avenger of his benefactor. He sponsored a man claiming to be Maurice's son Theodosius, who had supposedly escaped to Persia, and had him crowned by the catholicos. At the same time Narses, the Roman magister militum per Orientem and an old friend of Khosrow, refused to recognise Phocas, seized Edessa and appealed to Khosrow for help. Khosrow led his army in person, relieved Edessa, defeated the Roman general Germanus near Constantina (Germanus died of his wounds), defeated another Roman army at Arxamoun, and besieged Dara, which fell after nine months in 604. The war that followed lasted twenty-six years, the longest and most destructive of all Roman-Persian wars. In its first phase (603-610) the Persians conquered Roman Mesopotamia and Armenia; in the second (610-619) they took Syria, Palestine with Jerusalem (614), Egypt (619) and much of Anatolia, reaching Chalcedon. Historians debate Khosrow's aims: revenge for Maurice was a pretext, but the ambition of restoring the Achaemenid empire, or simply exploiting Roman weakness, explains the escalation. The war exhausted both empires and left them vulnerable to the Arab conquests of the 630s. The near-contemporary sources are the Armenian history attributed to Sebeos, the Chronicle of Khuzistan and the Chronicon Paschale; Theophanes, writing two centuries later, supplies much of the year-by-year chronology, not always reliably.

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)

set.detail: By 608 Phocas's regime was failing: the Persians were advancing in Mesopotamia and Armenia, his executions had alienated the aristocracy, and the circus factions, especially the Greens, were rioting in many cities. The revolt began in Africa, the richest and most secure province in the West. Heraclius the Elder, the exarch of Carthage, a veteran general of Maurice's Persian war of Armenian origin, and his brother Gregory, encouraged, according to some sources, by Priscus, Phocas's son-in-law and comes excubitorum, rebelled in 608, stopped the grain shipments to Constantinople, and struck coins showing himself and his son as consuls, without imperial insignia, a carefully ambiguous claim. Two expeditions were organised: Gregory's son Nicetas marched overland with an army of Moors and Romans to Egypt, the other granary of the capital, where he won the support of the population and the Greens and defeated Phocas's general Bonosus in 609-610, taking Alexandria. The younger Heraclius, the exarch's son, sailed with a fleet in 610, stopping at Thessalonica, the Aegean islands and Abydos, where he gathered supporters; his fleet carried icons of the Virgin on the masts. As he approached Constantinople, the excubitors under Priscus and the Greens deserted Phocas. On 5 October 610 Heraclius was crowned emperor and married Fabia-Eudokia; Phocas was executed after a famous exchange in which Heraclius asked him whether he had governed better, and he answered: 'will you do better?'. The revolt was the first time a provincial governor from the West overthrew an emperor in Constantinople, and it founded the Heraclian dynasty, which ruled until 711.

scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Olster, The Politics of Usurpation in the Seventh Century (1993)
Grierson, 'The consular coinage of Heraclius and the revolt against Phocas', DOP 6 (1950)

set.detail: Heraclius's fleet reached the Hebdomon on 3 October 610 after a voyage through the Aegean. Constantinople was ready to change sides: the Greens, whom Phocas had alienated by executions, burned parts of the city, and the comes excubitorum Priscus, Phocas's son-in-law, who had been in secret contact with the rebels, withdrew his support. Phocas's brother Domentziolus, guarding the Long Walls, fled. Phocas was seized by senators and by the Greens, stripped of the purple and brought to Heraclius on his ship. According to John of Antioch, Heraclius asked him 'Is this how you governed the state?' and Phocas replied 'Will you govern it better?'. Phocas was beheaded and his body mutilated; his head was paraded through the city, and his statue in the Hippodrome burned. His brother Domentziolus, the comes Orientis Bonosus and others were killed. On 5 October 610 the patriarch Sergius crowned Heraclius in the palace chapel of St Stephen, and on the same day married him to Fabia, renamed Eudokia, who was crowned Augusta. Heraclius, aged about 35, inherited a disastrous situation: the Persians had taken Mesopotamia and Armenia and were crossing the Euphrates into Syria and Anatolia, the Avars and Slavs were overrunning the Balkans, the army was demoralised and the treasury empty. Phocas's brother Comentiolus held out in Anatolia until 611. Heraclius's early years saw new defeats, including Antioch (613), Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (619). But his reign of 31 years would see the defeat of Persia (622-628) and then the loss of Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arabs (634-641). His accession marks the beginning of the Heraclian dynasty and is often taken as the beginning of the Byzantine empire proper.

scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Reinink and Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Haldon, Byzantium in the Seventh Century (1990)

set.detail: After the Persian capture of Caesarea in Cappadocia (611) and its recovery in 612, the Persians under Shahrbaraz attacked Syria, taking Apamea and Emesa in 611-612. In 613 Heraclius took the field in person, the first reigning emperor in two centuries to lead an army into battle, together with his brother Theodore and his cousin Nicetas, who brought troops from Egypt. The armies met near Antioch. The Romans had some initial success, but were then defeated by Shahrbaraz and Shahin; the Persians pursued them, and in a second battle in the Cilician Gates the Romans under Theodore were again defeated, though they inflicted heavy losses. Sebeos is the main source; Theophanes adds a few details. The defeat had serious consequences. It split the Roman East in two: the Persians took Antioch, cut off Syria and Palestine from Anatolia, captured Damascus and Tarsus, and opened the way to Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (618-619). When Shahin reached Chalcedon in 615, the Senate sent envoys to Khosrow with a letter, preserved by the Chronicon Paschale, which recognised Khosrow as the 'supreme emperor' and asked for peace; Khosrow had the envoys imprisoned and said he would not make peace until the Romans renounced Christ and worshipped the sun. For the next nine years Heraclius concentrated on reorganising the army and finances. The defeat at Antioch is significant as evidence of the military weakness of the empire after the revolt of Phocas, when the Roman field army had been greatly reduced by civil war, and as a lesson Heraclius learned for his later campaigns.

scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars II (2002)

set.detail: After the Roman defeat at Antioch in 613, the Persian army under Shahrbaraz marched south through Syria and Palestine, taking Caesarea Maritima, the provincial capital, without resistance. Jerusalem first agreed to submit, but an uprising killed the Persian officials left in the city. Shahrbaraz returned and besieged the city for about twenty days in April and May 614; according to the monk Antiochus Strategos, an eyewitness, the Persians undermined the walls with siege engines, broke in, and massacred the inhabitants, the dead being counted at 66,509 (later versions give other numbers) in the lists of the burial party led by one Thomas; Sebeos gives 57,000 dead and 35,000 captives. The patriarch Zacharias and many survivors were deported to Persia, with the relic of the True Cross, which was taken to Ctesiphon and given to the Christian queen Shirin. The churches of the Holy Sepulchre and others were burned. Christian sources accuse the Jews of helping the Persians and of massacring Christians at the Mamilla pool, but these claims, coloured by anti-Jewish polemic, have been questioned; excavations at Mamilla have found a mass grave with a chapel, consistent with the event. The Persians first entrusted Jerusalem to the Jews, then around 617 reversed this policy and allowed the abbot Modestus to restore the churches. The capture of the holy city and the loss of the True Cross shocked the Christian world and gave the war a religious character: Heraclius's campaigns from 622 were presented as a holy war, and the restoration of the Cross in 630 was its climax. The fall of Jerusalem is a central episode of apocalyptic literature, Christian and Jewish.
set.debate: Casualty figures and Jewish participation are disputed; archaeology suggests less destruction than the literary sources claim.

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Flusin, Saint Anastase le Perse et l'histoire de la Palestine (1992)
Avni, 'The Persian conquest of Jerusalem (614 CE): an archaeological assessment', BASOR 357 (2010)

set.detail: Egypt was the richest province of the empire and the source of the grain that fed Constantinople. After the fall of Jerusalem, Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt in 618, taking Pelusium and advancing into the Delta. Alexandria was besieged; the Roman governor Nicetas, Heraclius's cousin, and the Chalcedonian patriarch John the Almsgiver fled to Cyprus. The city fell in 619, according to the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria because a student named Peter showed the Persians a way in through the canal at the gate of the Sun, or because a defector opened a gate. The Persians massacred monks in the monasteries around Alexandria, according to Coptic sources, then advanced up the Nile, taking Upper Egypt by 621. Egypt remained under Persian rule for about ten years. Papyri in Pahlavi and Greek from Egypt show that the Persians maintained the existing tax administration, with Persian officials collecting the revenues and requisitioning supplies; the Coptic patriarch Andronicus remained in Alexandria, and the Persians appear to have favoured the Miaphysite majority over the Chalcedonians. The loss of Egypt had immediate consequences in Constantinople: the free bread distribution, introduced by Constantine in 332, was suspended in 618 and never restored, and Heraclius considered moving the capital to Carthage. Persian rule ended after the peace of 628-629, when Shahrbaraz withdrew under the agreement at Arabissus. The episode showed the vulnerability of Egypt, which would be conquered permanently by the Arabs barely ten years later, in 639-642, partly with the same Miaphysite resentment against Constantinople. The Persian occupation is thus a rehearsal for the Arab one.
set.debate: The date of the fall of Alexandria (618 or 619) is debated.

scholarship: Altheim-Stiehl, 'The Sasanians in Egypt', Bulletin de la Société d'Archéologie Copte 31 (1992)
Sänger, 'The administration of Sasanian Egypt', GRBS 51 (2011)
Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)

set.detail: After twelve years of defeats, with the Persians in control of Syria, Palestine and Egypt and raiding in Anatolia, and the Avars threatening the capital, Heraclius decided to take the offensive in person. He made peace with the Avars, paying a large subsidy, and financed the campaign with the treasures of the churches lent by the patriarch Sergius and by halving official salaries. On Easter Monday, 5 April 622, he left Constantinople, carrying an icon of Christ 'not made by human hands' (acheiropoietos), and crossed to Bithynia. He spent the summer training his army in the region of Pylae and in Cappadocia, according to George of Pisidia, whose poem Expeditio Persica describes the campaign: he held drills, mock battles and exercises, and improved discipline. In the autumn he marched east into Armenia or Pontus, threatening Persian communications, and drew Shahrbaraz into a battle in which the Persians were defeated, perhaps in the region of Cappadocia; George of Pisidia describes a solar eclipse and a ruse by which Heraclius lured the Persians out of an ambush position. The campaign is reconstructed differently by historians: Howard-Johnston places it in Pontus and Armenia, Kaegi in Cappadocia, and Zuckerman argues for a different chronology. In winter Heraclius returned to Constantinople because of an Avar threat. The campaign of 622 was the first victory of Heraclius over Persia and restored the morale of his army; it was presented as a holy war for the recovery of the True Cross. It also marked a change in imperial conduct, with the emperor commanding in person for years far from the capital.
set.debate: The route and location of the 622 victory are debated.

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, 'Heraclius' Persian campaigns and the revival of the East Roman Empire', War in History 6 (1999)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Zuckerman, 'Heraclius in 625', REB 60 (2002)

set.detail: According to the Muslim tradition, Muhammad, who had preached in Mecca since about 610, faced increasing hostility from the Quraysh after the deaths of his uncle and protector Abu Talib and his wife Khadija in 619. He sought support from other towns and tribes, and in 621 and 622, at Aqaba near Mecca, he made agreements with members of the Aws and Khazraj tribes from Yathrib, an oasis some 350 km to the north divided by long feuds, who invited him to come as arbiter. His followers emigrated in small groups during the summer of 622, and Muhammad himself, with Abu Bakr, left Mecca secretly, hiding in a cave on Mount Thawr to escape his pursuers, and arrived at Quba near Yathrib, traditionally on 24 September 622 (12 Rabi I). Yathrib became Madinat al-Nabi, the city of the Prophet, or simply Medina. There Muhammad organised the community (umma), building a mosque and agreeing a document, the so-called Constitution of Medina, preserved by Ibn Ishaq, which defined the rights and obligations of the emigrants (Muhajirun), the Medinan helpers (Ansar) and the Jewish tribes as a single community. The Hijra marked the transition of Muhammad from a persecuted preacher to the leader of a political community and military power. Under the caliph Umar, around 638, the year of the Hijra was adopted as the beginning of the Islamic calendar, its first day being 16 July 622. The traditional narrative depends on sources written more than a century later; non-Muslim contemporary sources say little about Muhammad before the conquests, and some revisionist historians have questioned the chronology.

scholarship: Watt, Muhammad at Medina (1956)
Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)
Lecker, The Constitution of Medina (2004)

set.detail: After a winter in Constantinople, Heraclius left on 25 March 624 with his wife Martina and marched through Cappadocia and Armenia to Theodosiopolis, then crossed into Persian Armenia, taking Dvin and Nakhchivan, and invaded Atropatene (Azerbaijan), the heartland of Persian religion. Khosrow II, who was at Ganzak with 40,000 men, fled before him. Heraclius took Ganzak and destroyed the city. He then advanced to the great fire temple of Adur Gushnasp, one of the three most sacred fires of Zoroastrianism, associated with the king and the warrior class, at Takht-i Suleiman (ancient Shiz, 'Thebarmais' in Greek sources), beside a volcanic lake; Theophanes says Heraclius extinguished the fire and destroyed the temple in revenge for Jerusalem, and that the treasures of Croesus were found there, a legend. Archaeological excavations at Takht-i Suleiman show a destruction layer of this period, although the sanctuary was later restored. Heraclius then turned north into Caucasian Albania for the winter, rather than returning to Roman territory, freeing, according to Theophanes, 50,000 prisoners, and recruited allies among the Lazi, Abasgians and Iberians. The campaign of 624 was a bold strategic innovation: instead of trying to recover Roman territory directly, Heraclius struck at the heart of the Persian empire, forcing Khosrow to withdraw his armies from Anatolia and Syria to defend Persia. It was also a religious war: the destruction of the fire temple answered the capture of the Cross in 614. Movses Daskhurantsi's history of the Albanians describes the arrival of Heraclius's army and its effect on the region.
set.debate: Whether the fire temple destroyed was at Takht-i Suleiman or elsewhere in Atropatene is debated.

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Naumann, Die Ruinen von Tacht-e Suleiman und Zendan-e Suleiman (1977)

set.detail: In 626, while Heraclius was in the Caucasus, Khosrow II and the Avar khagan agreed to attack Constantinople at the same time. Shahrbaraz marched across Anatolia and camped at Chalcedon opposite the capital, while the khagan advanced from the Balkans with an army of Avars, Slavs, Bulgars and Gepids, perhaps 80,000 strong. The defence was led by the patriarch Sergius and the patrician Bonus, magister officiorum, in the name of the young Constantine III; Heraclius sent 12,000 soldiers as reinforcement and remained in the East, sending his brother Theodore against Shahin. The siege began on 29 July 626. The Avars attacked the land walls with siege towers and catapults, particularly in the section near the gate of St Romanus. The defenders replied with artillery, and Sergius carried icons of the Virgin along the walls. On 7 August the Slavs, in monoxyla (dugout boats), tried to cross the Golden Horn to join the attack on the Blachernae area and to ferry Persian troops across the Bosporus; the Roman fleet destroyed them, and the sea was filled with corpses. The khagan, discouraged, burned his siege engines and withdrew on 8 August. Shahrbaraz withdrew to Syria. The defenders attributed the victory to the Virgin; the Akathistos hymn was later associated with this deliverance, and Theodore Syncellus preached a homily on the anniversary. The siege was a turning point: the failure weakened the Avars, whose subject peoples, Slavs and Bulgars, soon rebelled, and freed Heraclius to strike at the heart of Persia in 627. The Chronicon Paschale provides a day-by-day account.

sources.w: Homily on the Siege of Constantinople

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, 'The siege of Constantinople in 626', in Mango and Dagron (eds.), Constantinople and Its Hinterland (1995)
Pohl, The Avars (2018)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)

set.detail: In 627 Heraclius made an alliance with the Western Turks, whose army under Tong Yabghu's commander (called Ziebel in Byzantine sources) joined him at the siege of Tiflis. When the Turks withdrew in the autumn, Heraclius, with perhaps 25,000-50,000 men, including some Turks, marched south from the Caucasus in September 627 into Atropatene and then across the Zagros into Assyria, the heartland of the Persian empire, where no Roman army had been since Julian. Khosrow II sent an army under the general Rhahzadh (Roch Vehan), which followed the Romans. On 12 December 627, near the ruins of Nineveh, opposite Mosul, Heraclius turned and gave battle in the morning fog, which hid the Roman advance and neutralised the Persian archers. The battle lasted eleven hours. Heraclius, mounted on his horse Dorkon, fought in person, killing Rhahzadh in single combat, according to Theophanes, and two other Persian champions, and being wounded in the lip. The Persians lost 6,000 men and all their commanders, but did not flee, remaining near the battlefield overnight. The Romans captured 28 standards. Heraclius did not pursue but marched on toward Ctesiphon, plundering the royal palaces, including Dastagird, which Khosrow had abandoned, recovering 300 Roman standards. Khosrow fled to Ctesiphon, where he was overthrown by his son Kavad II in February 628. The battle of Nineveh, though not a crushing victory, destroyed the last Persian field army and Khosrow's prestige, and decided the war. Heraclius's own dispatch, read in Hagia Sophia, survives in the Chronicon Paschale, a rare first-person report of a Roman emperor on his campaign.

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, Witnesses to a World Crisis (2010)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)
Haldon, The Byzantine Wars (2001)

set.detail: After the defeat at Nineveh and the sack of Dastagird, Khosrow II retreated to Ctesiphon, refusing Heraclius's peace offers. His authority collapsed: he had alienated the nobility with executions and heavy taxes to finance the war, imprisoned many officials, and planned, according to some sources, to execute Shahrbaraz, who was still in Egypt and Syria. A conspiracy of nobles, including Shahrbaraz's son, the general Gurdanaspa and the sons of the executed Yazdin, freed prisoners and proclaimed Khosrow's son Kavad (Sheroe), born of the Christian Maria, king. Khosrow was arrested around 23-25 February 628, imprisoned in the 'House of Darkness' (or the house of a certain Maraspand), and executed a few days later, according to Tabari after being shown the corpses of his children; Kavad II also killed seventeen of his brothers. Heraclius learned of the coup in March near Ganzak, and Kavad II sent envoys to make peace. The terms, settled in April 628, were the return of all occupied Roman territory, the release of prisoners, and the return of the True Cross; Heraclius's dispatch from his camp, read in Hagia Sophia on 15 May 628, rejoiced that 'the arrogant Khosrow, enemy of God, has fallen'. The evacuation of Persian troops was slow, since Shahrbaraz refused to obey Kavad, and it was only in July 629 at Arabissus that Heraclius and Shahrbaraz agreed. Kavad II died of plague in September 628, and Persia fell into four years of civil war. Khosrow II, who had come closest of any Sasanian king to restoring the Achaemenid empire, ended in disaster.

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)

set.detail: The True Cross, taken from Jerusalem in 614 and kept at Ctesiphon, was returned by Shahrbaraz as part of the agreements of 629, possibly in exchange for Roman support for his usurpation. Heraclius took the relic in its case, with the seals still intact, and entered Jerusalem in a solemn procession on 21 March 630, through the Golden Gate, with his wife Martina, and restored it to the patriarch Modestus at the Holy Sepulchre. The date of 21 March 630 is given by Sebeos and Strategius; some historians, following a different reading of the sources, argue for 629. Later legend, celebrated in the liturgical feast of the Exaltation of the Cross on 14 September, claims that Heraclius was unable to pass through the gate until he had removed his royal clothes and walked barefoot, in humility, like Christ. The restoration was the high point of Heraclius's reign: he had defeated Persia, recovered the eastern provinces and the most sacred relic of Christendom, and in 629 had taken the title of basileus. At the same time, he ordered the Jews expelled from Jerusalem and its surroundings and, according to later sources, the forced baptism of Jews throughout the empire, in revenge for their alleged collaboration with the Persians. Within seven years, however, Jerusalem would surrender to the Arabs, and the Cross was taken to Constantinople in 636. The event became one of the most celebrated in medieval art and legend, and a model for crusading imagery; Piero della Francesca's frescoes in Arezzo show Heraclius defeating Khosrow and returning the Cross.

scholarship: Drijvers, 'Heraclius and the restitutio crucis', in Reinink and Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Zuckerman, 'Heraclius and the return of the Holy Cross', in Zuckerman (ed.), Constructing the Seventh Century (2013)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)

set.detail: According to the Muslim tradition, Muhammad, after leading the Farewell Pilgrimage to Mecca in March 632, fell ill with fever and headaches at Medina in the house of his wife Aisha, and died there on 8 June 632 (12 Rabi I 11 AH), aged about 62; he was buried in Aisha's room, now within the Mosque of the Prophet. At his death most of Arabia acknowledged his authority, through treaties with tribes and the conquest of Mecca in 630, and an expedition under the young Usama ibn Zayd was preparing to march to the Syrian frontier. He left no son and no clear provision for the succession. At a meeting in the hall (saqifa) of the Banu Sa'ida, the Medinan Ansar proposed one of their own leaders, but Umar and Abu Ubayda persuaded them to accept Abu Bakr, Muhammad's father-in-law and earliest supporter, as successor (khalifa). Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his supporters later contested this choice, the origin of the Sunni-Shia split. Many tribes considered their allegiance to have been personal to Muhammad and refused to pay the alms tax, while others followed rival prophets. Abu Bakr's response, the Ridda wars of 632-633, unified Arabia by force and created the army that invaded Syria and Iraq in 633-634. Some revisionist scholars point to the Doctrina Jacobi, a Greek text written in 634, which speaks of a prophet appearing among the Saracens, and to Christian sources implying that Muhammad led the first invasions, to question the traditional date; most historians accept 632.
set.debate: Shoemaker argues from non-Muslim sources that Muhammad may have been alive at the start of the conquest of Palestine.

scholarship: Watt, Muhammad at Medina (1956)
Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)
Shoemaker, The Death of a Prophet (2012)

set.detail: In 633 Abu Bakr sent four armies under Amr ibn al-As, Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, Shurahbil ibn Hasana and Abu Ubayda to Syria, where they met growing Roman resistance. Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had conquered al-Hira and the lower Euphrates in Iraq in 633, was ordered to reinforce them. To arrive quickly and by surprise, he chose the most direct route across the desert from Iraq to Syria. The tradition, preserved in Tabari, Baladhuri and others, describes the march: Khalid, with perhaps 500 to 800 picked men (later traditions say up to 9,000), crossed from Qurraqir to Suwa, a five-day march without water, guided by Rafi ibn Umayra of the Tayy tribe; the camels were made to drink large amounts before setting off, and some were slaughtered on the way so that the water in their stomachs could be given to the horses. When the guide, nearly blind, found the hidden spring at Suwa by the smell of a boxthorn, the army survived. Khalid emerged near Palmyra, which surrendered, raided the Ghassanids at Marj Rahit on Easter Sunday, and joined the Muslim armies near Bostra, which he helped take. The route is debated: a northern route through the Euphrates valley and Palmyra, a central route through the desert, and a southern route via Dumat al-Jandal have been proposed. The march, which probably took place in spring 634, is famous as a feat of endurance, but it was also strategically important: it brought the most experienced Muslim commander to Syria before the decisive battles of Ajnadayn, Fahl and the Yarmuk, and surprised the Romans, who did not expect an army from the desert.
set.debate: The route, date and size of the force are disputed.

scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

set.detail: The first major battle between the Arabs and a Roman field army took place at Ajnadayn, between Ramla and Beit Guvrin (Eleutheropolis) in southern Palestine, traditionally on 30 July 634 (28 Jumada I 13 AH). After the Arab victory at Dathin near Gaza in February 634, in which the Roman commander Sergius was killed, Heraclius, then at Emesa, sent an army under his brother Theodore (or under a commander named in Arabic sources as Wardan) to Palestine. The Arab armies in Syria, under Amr ibn al-As, Yazid, Shurahbil and Abu Ubayda, combined with the forces of Khalid ibn al-Walid, who had just arrived from Iraq, and gave battle. The Muslim tradition reports heavy fighting, a Roman defeat and the flight of the Roman army to Jerusalem, Gaza, Caesarea and Damascus, with Arab losses including several notable Companions. Numbers are uncertain: later traditions give 100,000 Romans, an impossible figure; modern estimates are of the order of 10,000-20,000 on each side. Christian sources say little about the battle; the Chronicle of 640 by Thomas the Presbyter records a battle between the Romans and the 'Arabs of Muhammad' in February 634 near Gaza (Dathin), and Theophanes mentions the defeat of Theodore. The victory opened Palestine to the Arabs, who besieged its cities, and led Heraclius to send another army, defeated at Fahl in early 635. The exact location and the identity of the Roman commander are debated; some scholars have suggested that Ajnadayn and the Yarmuk have been confused in the tradition. The battle marks the beginning of the Arab conquest of Roman Syria.
set.debate: Date, location and Roman command are disputed; the date of 30 July 634 is traditional.

scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)

set.detail: After their victories at Ajnadayn (634) and Marj al-Saffar, the Arab armies blockaded Damascus, the main city of Phoenicia Libanensis, from about March 635. The siege lasted about six months. The city, with strong walls and a garrison, was cut off from outside help after the Roman relief army was defeated at Fahl (Pella) in January 635. According to the Muslim tradition, the city surrendered in September 635 under negotiations conducted by the bishop or the fiscal official Mansur ibn Sarjun, grandfather of John of Damascus, with Khalid ibn al-Walid, who agreed to spare the lives and property of the inhabitants, their churches and their walls in return for the payment of tribute (jizya), at one dinar and a measure of wheat per head. Another tradition says that Khalid entered the eastern gate by assault at night while Abu Ubayda accepted the surrender at the western gate, leading to a dispute over whether the city had been taken by force or by treaty, which affected the legal status of its property; the jurists settled that it was by treaty. As the Roman counter-offensive that ended at the Yarmuk approached in 636, the Arabs temporarily evacuated Damascus, returning after the victory. Damascus became the capital of the Umayyad caliphate under Mu'awiya, governor of Syria from 639 and caliph from 661. Its Christian population remained in the majority for a long time; the cathedral of St John was shared, according to tradition, until the caliph al-Walid I built the Great Mosque in 705-715. The surrender of Damascus is a classic example of the negotiated capitulations that marked the conquest of Syria.
set.debate: Whether Damascus was taken by treaty or force, and the date (635 or 636), are debated in the Arabic sources.

scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

set.detail: After the fall of Damascus and Emesa in 635-636, Heraclius, based in Antioch, assembled the largest army he could raise to recover Syria: regular troops, Armenians under Vahan (the commander-in-chief), troops under the sakellarios Theodore Trithyrios, Christian Arabs of the Ghassanid king Jabala ibn al-Ayham, and Slavs. Numbers are uncertain; Arab sources speak of 200,000 or more, modern estimates range from 15,000-20,000 to 40,000-50,000. The Arab armies, perhaps 20,000-30,000, evacuated Emesa and Damascus and concentrated south of the Golan, near the Yarmuk river and its tributary the Wadi al-Ruqqad. After weeks of manoeuvres and skirmishes in which the Romans were weakened by quarrels between Vahan and Theodore, a mutiny of the Armenians who proclaimed Vahan emperor according to Theophanes, and the desertion of Christian Arabs, the decisive battle took place over several days, ending on 20 August 636 (12 Rajab 15 AH). The Arab tradition describes a series of attacks in which the Muslim women at the rear drove back fleeing men, and a final cavalry charge by Khalid that separated the Roman cavalry from the infantry; the Roman infantry was driven into the ravines of the Wadi al-Ruqqad, where many died. A dust storm blowing in the faces of the Romans is also mentioned. Vahan and Theodore were killed. The defeat was decisive: Heraclius abandoned Syria, the Roman army never again faced the Arabs in a pitched battle in Syria, and Jerusalem, Antioch, Aleppo and Caesarea fell within four years. Theophanes and the Arabic sources agree on the outcome, if on little else, and the battle was remembered on both sides as the moment Syria was lost.
set.debate: Numbers, the command structure and the exact sequence of the battle are debated.

scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Nicolle, Yarmuk 636 AD (1994)
Jandora, 'The battle of the Yarmuk: a reconstruction', Journal of Asian History 19 (1985)

set.detail: Jerusalem, whose patriarch Sophronius had lamented in his Christmas sermon of 634 that the Saracens prevented Christians from going to Bethlehem, was blockaded by the Arabs under Amr ibn al-As or Abu Ubayda from 636, after the Yarmuk. Its garrison and people held out, apparently for several months, until Sophronius agreed to surrender on condition that the caliph Umar come in person to accept it, according to the Muslim tradition and Theophanes. Umar travelled from Medina to al-Jabiya in the Golan, where he organised the administration of Syria, and then entered Jerusalem in 637 or 638, dressed in a simple camel-hair garment, according to Theophanes, who calls his appearance 'diabolical pretence'. The terms, known in a later version as the Covenant of Umar, guaranteed the lives, property and churches of the inhabitants in return for the jizya, and, according to Tabari's version, excluded Jews from residing in the city; some versions of the tradition say Jews were allowed to return, which they had been forbidden since Hadrian, with limited exceptions. Sophronius showed Umar the Holy Sepulchre, where, according to a later legend, Umar refused to pray to prevent the church being turned into a mosque. Umar visited the Temple Mount, then a rubbish dump, and ordered it cleared; a simple mosque was built there, which the Gallic pilgrim Arculf described around 680, and which was replaced by the Dome of the Rock in 691-692. Sophronius died soon after the surrender, in 638 or 639. The capture of Jerusalem gave the new Muslim community control of a city sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims.
set.debate: Date (637 or 638) and the authenticity of the terms are debated.

scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Gil, A History of Palestine 634-1099 (1992)
Levy-Rubin, Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire (2011)

set.detail: After the conquest of Syria and Palestine, Amr ibn al-As, who had traded in Egypt before Islam according to the tradition, persuaded the caliph Umar, who was meeting the commanders at al-Jabiya, to allow him to invade Egypt; Umar, the tradition says, sent a letter ordering him to turn back if he had not yet crossed the border, which Amr opened only after entering Egypt. Amr left Caesarea or Gaza in December 639 with perhaps 3,500-4,000 men, mostly from the tribes of Akk and Ghafiq, crossed Sinai and celebrated the Feast of the Sacrifice at al-Arish. He besieged Pelusium (al-Farama) for about a month, taking it in early 640, and advanced through the eastern Delta to Bilbeis, which fell after a month, and then to the fortress of Babylon near Memphis at the head of the Delta, where he camped in spring 640. Egypt was defended by a considerable Roman army under the commander Theodore and the governor of Arcadia and others, but divided by rivalries and by the hostility of the Coptic population toward the Chalcedonian patriarch Cyrus (al-Muqawqis), who had persecuted the Miaphysites since 631. John of Nikiu, a Coptic bishop writing at the end of the seventh century, is the principal non-Arab source, describing in vivid detail the indecision of the Roman commanders, the atrocities of the conquerors, and the collaboration of some Egyptians. Arab sources, especially Ibn Abd al-Hakam's Futuh Misr, are much later and contain legendary elements. The conquest of Egypt, completed with the capitulation of Alexandria in 641-642, deprived the empire of its richest province and its grain supply, and gave the Arabs a base for the conquest of North Africa and a fleet.

scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902; 2nd ed. 1978)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Booth, 'The Muslim conquest of Egypt reconsidered', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013)

set.detail: In spring 640 Amr ibn al-As, with perhaps 4,000 men, was encamped near the fortress of Babylon, unable to take it, and asked the caliph Umar for reinforcements. Umar sent some 4,000 men under al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, a cousin of Muhammad, which arrived in June 640, bringing the Arab army to about 12,000-15,000. The Roman army of Egypt under Theodore, supreme commander, which had concentrated at Babylon, came out to give battle near Heliopolis (Ayn Shams), north of Babylon, in July 640. According to the Arab tradition, Amr divided his army into three: the main force faced the Romans, while two detachments, one hidden at Umm Dunayn on the Nile and another in the hills to the east, attacked the Romans from behind during the battle. The Romans broke and fled, some to Babylon and others to Nikiu downstream. John of Nikiu reports the battle as a Roman defeat caused by the indecision of the commanders, and describes the subsequent capture of the fort of Umm Dunayn and of Fayyum. The victory gave the Arabs control of the region around Babylon and Memphis and allowed them to begin a regular siege of the fortress, which surrendered in April 641. Heliopolis was the decisive field battle of the conquest of Egypt: after it, the Roman army did not again risk a pitched battle in Egypt and confined itself to defending fortified cities, especially Alexandria, while divisions within the Roman leadership deepened after the death of Heraclius in February 641. The tactical model of the hidden detachments resembles accounts of other battles in the conquest literature and may be partly literary.

scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1978)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

set.detail: Heraclius died in Constantinople on 11 February 641, aged about 66, after a reign of over thirty years. In his last years, after the loss of Syria, he lived mostly in the palace of Hieria on the Asian shore, suffering, according to Nikephoros, from a fear of water (he crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats screened with branches so as not to see the sea) and from a disease, perhaps dropsy, in which his genitals turned back on themselves so that his urine sprayed his face, a punishment, according to contemporaries, for his incestuous marriage to his niece Martina. His last years were dominated by the Arab conquests, the failure of his religious policy (the Ekthesis of 638, which Pope John IV condemned), conspiracies, including one in 637 led by his illegitimate son Athalarichos, who was mutilated and exiled, and the struggle for succession between Constantine III, his son by Eudokia, and Heraclonas, his son by Martina. His will named Constantine III and Heraclonas co-emperors with equal rights, with Martina as their mother and empress, a solution which led to a crisis: Constantine III died in May 641, perhaps poisoned, and Heraclonas and Martina were overthrown in September-October 641 in favour of Constantine III's son Constans II. Heraclius was buried in the church of the Holy Apostles. His reign is one of the most paradoxical in Roman history: he saved the empire from Persia in a brilliant war and restored the True Cross, but lost the eastern provinces to the Arabs within a decade. Historians also attribute to his reign the beginning of administrative changes, such as the use of Greek as the language of government and the title of basileus.

scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Reinink and Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Haldon, Byzantium in the Seventh Century (1990)

set.detail: The fortress of Babylon, a Roman stronghold built under Trajan and rebuilt under Diocletian on the right bank of the Nile, at the point where the river divides into the Delta (in present-day Old Cairo), controlled river traffic between Upper and Lower Egypt. Its massive walls and towers, parts of which survive under the Hanging Church and the Coptic Museum, were defended by a large garrison. After the battle of Heliopolis in July 640, Amr ibn al-As besieged it from September 640. According to the tradition, the Roman patriarch and governor Cyrus negotiated with Amr, agreeing to pay tribute, but Heraclius rejected the agreement and recalled Cyrus to Constantinople, where he was accused of treason. The siege lasted seven months. The defenders were weakened by disease and by news of the death of Heraclius in February 641, which removed hope of reinforcements. The Arabs finally stormed or forced the surrender of the fortress on Easter Monday, 9 April 641 (or Good Friday, 6 April), al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam leading an assault over the walls, according to some traditions. The garrison was allowed to leave by river for Nikiu and Alexandria. Amr's camp near the fortress became the garrison city of Fustat, the new capital of Egypt and later the core of Cairo, where Amr built the first mosque in Africa in 641-642. The fall of Babylon opened the Delta and the way to Alexandria. John of Nikiu describes the fall and the atrocities that followed in the towns of the Delta, including Nikiu, where the inhabitants were massacred in May 641.
set.debate: The date (Good Friday or Easter Monday 641) and whether it was taken by storm or treaty are debated.

scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1978)
Sheehan, Babylon of Egypt: The Archaeology of Old Cairo (2010)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

set.detail: After the death of Heraclius in February 641, a power struggle in Constantinople between Constantine III, Heraclonas and Martina paralysed imperial policy. Martina's regime, seeking peace on the eastern front, restored Cyrus, the former Chalcedonian patriarch, who had negotiated with Amr in 640 and had been exiled by Heraclius, and sent him back to Alexandria in September 641 with full powers to make peace. Cyrus travelled to Babylon, where he met Amr, and signed a treaty on 8 November 641. According to John of Nikiu, the principal source, the terms were: an armistice of eleven months to allow the Roman troops to evacuate Alexandria by sea with their property; payment of a tribute (poll tax) of two dinars per adult male, plus a land tax; the delivery of 150 soldiers and 50 civilians as hostages; the Arabs undertaking not to seize churches or interfere with Christians; and the Jews allowed to remain in Alexandria. When the Alexandrians learned of the treaty they rioted against Cyrus, who persuaded them that it was the best option. The Roman garrison left Alexandria on 17 September 642, and Amr entered the city. Cyrus had died in March 642. The treaty marked the end of nearly a thousand years of Greek and Roman rule in Egypt since Alexander. In 645-646 a Roman fleet under Manuel briefly recovered Alexandria, but Amr retook it in 646. The well-known story that Amr burned the Library of Alexandria on Umar's orders appears only in thirteenth-century sources and is generally considered a legend. The treaty's terms, known mainly from John of Nikiu, became a model for later conquests.
